title: Good, well, fast, hard, late and hardly
summary: Choose good or well for qualities, performance and health; recognise when fast, hard and late work without -ly; and distinguish hard from hardly, late from lately, and almost-negative expressions such as hardly any and hardly ever.
learningObjectives: Distinguish the adjective good from the adverb well and recognise well as an adjective for health.
Use well with selected past participles and recognise natural expressions such as well-known and well-written.
Use fast, hard and late as both adjectives and adverbs without adding -ly.
Distinguish hard from hardly and late from lately in context.
Place hardly naturally and use hardly any, hardly anybody, hardly anything and hardly ever to express very small amounts or frequency.

explanation.heading: Good describes quality; well usually describes performance
explanation.body: Good is an adjective, so it can describe a person, thing or result: a good design. Well is normally the adverb used after an action verb to tell us how effectively someone acts: she designed it well. Well also works as an adjective meaning healthy, especially after feel or be. A person can be good at an activity but do it well.
explanation.example: The singer gave a good performance and sang remarkably well.

explanation.heading: Well before selected past participles
explanation.body: Well combines naturally with many past participles to describe the standard of preparation or a quality: well-organised, well-informed, well-paid and well-known. The combination can be placed before a noun, often with a hyphen, or after a linking verb. This construction describes quality or degree rather than a separate new tense.
explanation.example: We attended a well-organised conference with clear signs at every entrance.

explanation.heading: Fast, hard and late have no separate -ly manner form
explanation.body: Fast, hard and late can be adjectives or adverbs with the same spelling. A fast bicycle can travel fast; a hard task can make someone work hard; a late arrival means someone arrived late. In these meanings, do not invent fastly or use hardly as the adverb of hard.
explanation.example: The courier drove fast but still arrived late.

explanation.heading: Hard and hardly have opposite practical meanings
explanation.body: Work hard means make a strong effort. Hardly means almost not or very little, and it usually appears before the main verb or before a word such as any. Saying someone hardly worked means they did almost no work, not that they worked with great effort. Can hardly often signals that an action is extremely difficult or almost impossible.
explanation.example: Even with the lights on, we could hardly see the labels.

explanation.heading: Lately refers to a recent period
explanation.body: Late means after the expected time: the coach arrived late. Lately means recently or during the recent period, often with the present perfect: I haven’t travelled much lately. They are not interchangeable, even though they share a root.
explanation.example: I have been going to bed earlier lately, so I am rarely late for work.

explanation.heading: Hardly any, hardly ever and other near-negative expressions
explanation.body: Hardly any means almost no amount or number; hardly anyone or anybody means almost nobody, and hardly anything means almost nothing. Hardly ever means almost never. These expressions already have near-negative force, so a further ordinary not is generally unnecessary. Hardly can also mean certainly not in judgements such as hardly surprising, but focus first on its everyday amount and frequency meanings.
explanation.example: There is hardly any room on the commuter train, and we hardly ever find a seat.

left.label: Adjective: good
left.note: Good describes the quality of the explanation.

right.label: Adverb: well
right.note: Well describes the way she performed the action.

right.label: Hardly: almost not
right.note: Hardly suggests they did very little work.

left.label: Late
left.note: Late describes arrival after the expected time.

right.label: Lately
right.example: The buses have been unreliable lately.
right.note: Lately refers to a period extending into the recent past.

examples.sentence: After the training course, Fatima can handle customer questions well.
examples.note: Well describes how effectively Fatima handles questions.

examples.sentence: Our neighbour is not well today, so she is resting at home.
examples.note: Well describes the neighbour’s health, so it functions as an adjective.

examples.sentence: The guide is well-written and easy to follow.
examples.note: Well-written describes the quality of the completed text.

examples.sentence: You need to work hard to meet the deadline.
examples.note: Hard is the adverb of effort; hardly would change the meaning.

examples.sentence: The museum closes late on Fridays, but I have not visited it lately.
examples.note: Late refers to the closing time; lately means recently.

examples.sentence: Hardly anybody knew the answer, and there was hardly any time left.
examples.note: Hardly anybody and hardly any indicate very small numbers and amounts.

commonMistakes.incorrect: She communicates very good with clients.
commonMistakes.correct: She communicates very well with clients.
commonMistakes.why: An adverb describes how she communicates; well is the adverb paired with good.

commonMistakes.incorrect: We had to work hardly to finish the repairs.
commonMistakes.correct: We had to work hard to finish the repairs.
commonMistakes.why: Hard means with great effort; hardly would mean almost not.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The team has not held a meeting late.
commonMistakes.correct: The team has not held a meeting lately.
commonMistakes.why: Lately means recently; late refers to a time after what was expected.

commonMistakes.incorrect: There was hardly some space to move.
commonMistakes.correct: There was hardly any space to move.
commonMistakes.why: The near-negative hardly normally combines with any, not some, in this quantity expression.
Hardly usually appears before an ordinary main verb such as understand.

studyTips: Compare paired sentences aloud: a good speaker / speaks well; works hard / hardly works; arrives late / has not visited lately.
When you see hardly, paraphrase it as almost not and check that the sentence still matches the intended meaning.
Practise the chunks hardly any time, hardly anybody, can hardly see and hardly ever, rather than learning hardly by itself.

exercises.prompt: The new employee handled the customer complaint ___.
exercises.feedback: Well is the adverb describing how effectively the employee handled the complaint.

exercises.prompt: The fog is so thick that we can ___ see the road.
exercises.feedback: Hardly means almost not; can hardly see describes extreme difficulty seeing.

exercises.prompt: I haven’t spoken to my former manager ___, but I hope to call soon.
exercises.feedback: Lately means recently, which matches the period leading up to now.

exercises.prompt: The instructions were ___, so even beginners understood the procedure.
exercises.feedback: Well-written is an idiomatic combination with a past participle describing quality.

exercises.prompt: I had a fever yesterday, but I feel ___ today. (good/well; write the adjective meaning healthy)
exercises.feedback: Well can function as an adjective meaning healthy after feel.

exercises.prompt: Mila ___ ever misses her morning run. (almost never; one word)
Even with my glasses, I can ___ read the tiny instructions. (almost cannot; one word)
exercises.feedback: Can hardly read expresses extreme difficulty and places hardly before the main verb.

exercises.prompt: The last bus arrived ___ because of heavy traffic. (after the scheduled time; one word)
exercises.feedback: Late is also an adverb; it describes arriving after the expected time.

exercises.prompt: Correct the wrong adverb; the workers made a great effort: They worked hardly to finish before noon.
acceptedAnswers: They worked hard to finish before noon.
exercises.feedback: Hard shows strong effort, while hardly means almost not.

exercises.prompt: Correct the time expression; the speaker means recently: We have not seen our neighbours late.
acceptedAnswers: We have not seen our neighbours lately.
exercises.feedback: Lately means recently and works with the present perfect in this context.

exercises.prompt: Correct the position of hardly: I can see hardly the road signs in this rain.
acceptedAnswers: I can hardly see the road signs in this rain.
exercises.feedback: Put hardly before the ordinary main verb see.

exercises.prompt: Correct the determiner after hardly: There is hardly some water in the tank.
acceptedAnswers: There is hardly any water in the tank.
exercises.feedback: Hardly any means almost no amount and is the natural phrase here.

speakingExercises.prompt: The technician repaired the machine successfully. Say one sentence starting “The technician” and ending “well”, using repaired the machine.
acceptedAnswers: The technician repaired the machine well.
speakingExercises.feedback: Well describes how effectively the repair was done.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say one sentence about a recognised author. Begin “The author is” and end “well-known”.
speakingExercises.feedback: Well-known is an established description of someone recognised by many people.

speakingExercises.prompt: You have met Nina only once. Say one complete sentence beginning “I” and using hardly know Nina.
speakingExercises.feedback: Hardly know means know very little about someone.

speakingExercises.prompt: Paraphrase “I have not visited the office recently.” Begin “I have not” and end “lately”.
acceptedAnswers: I have not visited the office lately.
I haven't visited the office lately.
speakingExercises.feedback: Lately can replace recently when referring to the recent period.

speakingExercises.prompt: Correct only the adverb in this sentence to express strong effort: “We worked hardly all morning.” Say the corrected complete sentence.
speakingExercises.feedback: Hard indicates effort; hardly would mean almost not.

speakingExercises.prompt: The room was so dark that seeing the screen was almost impossible. Start “I could” and use “hardly see the screen”.
acceptedAnswers: I could hardly see the screen.
speakingExercises.feedback: Could hardly expresses near inability in the past.

speakingExercises.prompt: Produce exactly two sentences using these facts, in this order: the team / work hard / all day; they / hardly rest. Use past simple and begin with “The team”.
acceptedAnswers: The team worked hard all day. They hardly rested.
speakingExercises.feedback: Worked hard shows effort; hardly rested shows that they rested very little.

speakingExercises.prompt: A colleague asks how your father is feeling. He has recovered and is healthy now. Reply in one sentence beginning “He” and ending “well now”. Use is.
speakingExercises.feedback: Well after is can describe being in good health.

listeningExercises.audioText: Mara worked hard all afternoon, but she hardly made any progress on the report.
listeningExercises.feedback: Worked hard shows effort; hardly made any progress describes the disappointing result.

listeningExercises.audioText: The train arrived late, but the conductor explained the delay very well.
choices: The explanation was poor and the train was on time.
The train was delayed and the explanation was effective.
The conductor arrived early and said nothing.
listeningExercises.feedback: Late describes the train arrival; well describes the quality of the explanation.

listeningExercises.audioText: I have not spoken to the sales team lately.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the single word at the end of the sentence that means recently.
listeningExercises.feedback: Lately means recently, not after the scheduled time.

listeningExercises.audioText: The instructions were written well, but the print was so small I could hardly read them.
listeningExercises.prompt: What prevented the speaker from reading easily?
choices: The poor quality of the explanation.
listeningExercises.feedback: The speaker says the instructions were written well but the small print made reading difficult.

listeningExercises.audioText: Our new colleague is well known in the industry, but she hardly ever attends conferences.
listeningExercises.prompt: How often does the colleague attend conferences?

listeningExercises.audioText: The children played well during the match, but they were tired because they had trained hard yesterday.
choices: They played badly in the match.
They had made a strong effort in training.
listeningExercises.feedback: Trained hard expresses considerable effort the day before.

listeningExercises.audioText: We have hardly any bread left for breakfast.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two words heard immediately before “bread”.
listeningExercises.feedback: Hardly any means almost no bread is left.

listeningExercises.audioText: The bus arrived late because of roadworks.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word verb phrase heard immediately after “The bus”.
listeningExercises.feedback: Arrived late describes reaching the destination after the scheduled time.
